notes.description: timeupdate fires about four times a second. A half second linear transition on left is what turns those steps into continuous travel.

notes.label: stopPropagation is load-bearing
notes.description: Without it a click on the strip would seek and then bubble to the root handler and pause the video in the same gesture.

entries.check: The video plays above a strip of stills, the red playhead advances along it, clicks on the strip jump the footage to new shots, and the Pause and Play label appears on the frame clicks.

entries.name: scatter-letter-intro
entries.title: Scatter Letter Intro
entries.description: A landing sequence where a wordmark assembles, counts itself in, then scatters. The letters rise into place on a stagger, a three two one counter steps a single strip by exactly one line height per beat, and when it lands the type blows up to fifteen percent of the frame while six black panels wipe away in a random order to expose the video behind. In the same instant each letter is thrown to its own hand-authored vertical offset, so the wordmark comes apart into a composition rather than dispersing evenly. The letters use mix-blend-mode difference, so they invert against whatever the footage puts behind them.

notes.label: The scatter is authored, not random
notes.description: Each letter has its own final offset in the movements array. A random spread would look arbitrary; these values are a composition.

notes.label: The counter is one strip
notes.description: 3, 2 and 1 are a single element stepped by exactly one line height per beat, so the digits can never drift out of register with each other.

notes.label: Letters invert against the footage
notes.description: mix-blend-mode difference means the wordmark reacts to whatever the video puts behind it, so it stays legible over both light and dark frames without a scrim.

entries.check: The yellow wordmark holds while the counter steps 3, 2, 1, then the letters scatter to their own offsets over the hero video as the black panels clear, inverting against the footage.

entries.name: pixel-cube-avatar
entries.title: Pixel Cube Avatar
entries.description: A wireframe cube rasterized onto a 17 by 17 pixel grid with RGB channel separation. Twelve edges are projected through a two-axis rotation and drawn with an integer Bresenham line into three 8-bit channel buffers; the red and blue passes sit a few degrees off green and scale slightly apart, so the wireframe splits into chromatic fringes, and each frame blends the last one back in so motion smears a decaying trail. It idles still, spins on hover, follows a drag, coasts on release, and returns on a randomized spring to whichever of two rest poses is nearer. A click fires a multi-turn tumble with a decaying sine wobble on top. Canvas 2D and one rAF loop, no dependencies.

notes.label: The grid stays 17 by 17 at every size
notes.description: Resolution is what makes it read as pixels, so size scales the block each cell draws rather than adding cells. A larger avatar is the same 289-cell simulation with bigger squares.

notes.label: Chroma reacts to speed, not to a clock
notes.description: The red and blue passes are offset by a fixed 13 degrees plus a term driven by how fast the cube actually turned this frame, clamped to 0.4 radians. Standing still it is nearly clean; thrown hard it tears into full RGB.

notes.label: The trail is a max blend, not alpha
notes.description: Each frame keeps the brighter of the new edge and 90 percent of the previous one per channel, so the smear decays without ever muddying the live wireframe underneath it.

notes.label: Two rest poses, nearest one wins
notes.description: On release it measures the angular distance to both head-on orientations and springs to the closer one, with the spring frequency softened the further it has to travel, so a long throw settles slowly and a nudge snaps back.

entries.check: The chromatic pixel cube idles, turns under the drag, then tumbles through several orientations with RGB fringing after the click.

entries.name: phatake
entries.title: Phatake
entries.description: Diwali crackers on the BLANK Interfaces logo, as an isometric pixel diorama. The logo is extruded into a black slab on a sandstone courtyard with a rangoli and diyas, and kept as a heightmap with soot and litter grids so every cracker leaves a mark. Tap a spot on the logo and the nearest of three children, in a lehenga, a kurta and a Nehru jacket, runs over, crouches to light the next cracker with an agarbatti, runs off and covers their ears. Sutli bombs break chunks out of the slab down to the cut stone, rockets climb off it and burst (one in four skids across instead), anaar fountains and chakris scorch it, and ladis litter it with red paper. Twelve crackers a round; after the last one a tap sweeps the logo clean. A 360 by 280 software rasteriser with a depth buffer, Bayer dither, hue-shifted ramps and long screen-right shadows, scaled by whole device pixels. Renders only the canvas, pauses off screen, synthesizes its sounds. Renderer ported from Pixel Plays (MIT). No dependencies.

notes.label: The logo is a heightmap, not a sprite
notes.description: The BLANK Interfaces paths are rasterized once into a slab mask and a letter mask, then the slab lives as a 0.1-unit height grid with soot and litter beside it. Bombs lower cells and drop the thin ones to zero, so breaks chip the real outline and expose sandy cut stone on the walls that face the camera.

notes.label: Two floors for shadows
notes.description: Ground-plane shadows only land on ground pixels, and the slab top is excluded from them. Children cast onto whatever height they stand on through a second mask, so their shadows sit on the logo instead of sliding off to the courtyard below.

notes.label: Soot is grain, not dither
notes.description: Soot and ash use a per-pixel hash instead of the Bayer matrix, because an ordered pattern on black reads as a checkerboard. Litter never settles in a fresh break, so craters keep a clean cut-stone form.

notes.label: Rebakes, not redraws
notes.description: The courtyard, slab and static shadows are baked into one buffer and rebaked at most every 100 ms when something changes. A frame only adds the children, crackers, sparks and smoke on top.

notes.label: Whole-pixel scaling
notes.description: The 360 by 280 canvas is scaled by a whole number of device pixels to fit the container and drawn with pixelated rendering, so no pixel is ever interpolated.

entries.check: Crackers light on the BLANK Interfaces slab with small sparks and smoke, leaving soot marks across the isometric courtyard.

entries.name: pixel-cube-field
entries.title: Pixel Cube Field
entries.description: A grid of RGB-split wireframe cubes that aim at the cursor. Each cube is rasterized the same way as the single Pixel Cube Avatar, twelve edges drawn with an integer Bresenham line into three 8-bit channel buffers with the red and blue passes offset a few degrees from green, and the whole field shares one cell buffer and one canvas. Orientation comes from each cube's offset to the pointer: the cube under the cursor sits head-on and the tilt grows outward, saturating at a set radius, so the grid reads as a lens aimed wherever the mouse is. Cubes are never scaled by distance, so the field stays flat rather than bulging. Every cube eases independently, the fringing widens with how fast each one turned, the focus drifts by itself after three idle seconds, and a click sends a ring of full revolutions outward from the cube you hit. No dependencies.

notes.label: Tilt grows outward, not inward
notes.description: The cube under the cursor is the one held head-on and every other cube leans by its offset to it, so the field points at the pointer instead of peaking there. The offset vector is clamped to one radius rather than the angle being clamped, which keeps the lean direction correct at the far corners instead of flattening them.

notes.label: Flat by construction
notes.description: Cubes are never scaled or translated by distance from the focus, only rotated, so the grid reads as a field of turning objects rather than a bulging lens.

notes.label: One canvas for the whole grid
notes.description: Every cube rasterizes into the same three channel buffers and the field is flushed with a single putImageData, so 36 cubes cost one canvas and one rAF loop instead of 36 of each.

notes.label: Per-cube chroma and easing
notes.description: Each cube carries its own rotation, its own half-life easing and its own chroma offset, so they lag into place independently and only the ones actually turning fast tear into full RGB.

notes.label: The ripple is one full turn
notes.description: A click spins each ring by exactly 2 pi on an ease-out, so every cube lands back where it started and the wave leaves no drift behind it.

entries.check: The grid of RGB-fringed wireframe cubes changes orientation across the field as the pointer moves, with cubes near it head-on and outer ones leaning.

entries.name: liquid-glass-carousel
entries.title: Liquid Glass Carousel
entries.description: An infinite row of image panels drawn through a liquid-glass lens. The carousel renders into an offscreen buffer at device resolution and a fullscreen quad resamples it through a shader that combines an elliptical mask, an inward pull, per-channel chromatic dispersion, a fluid rim wave from two sine harmonics, a central nova, and a shimmering accent ring. Panels share one height and take their width from each image's measured aspect, so nothing is cropped, and the row loops by wrapping a single scroll value against the summed slot widths. Wheel input moves a target the scroll lerps toward, and once the wheel goes quiet the target is redirected onto the nearest panel center so the row settles on an image inside the same glide. Scroll speed shrinks every panel by up to a quarter while it moves. Clicking a panel glides it to center and opens focus: it scales up, the lens distortion fades out, and every other panel sweeps down in a center-out wave. On load the panels rise from below at 80px tall, hold, then grow to full size while the lens blooms in. Three.js with GSAP.

notes.label: One scroll value, no clones to manage
notes.description: The row loops by wrapping a single scroll number against the summed slot widths, then pushing each pooled mesh out by its repetition rung. Four copies of the set exist so a wide viewport never runs dry, and any panel copy can be addressed by an unbounded integer index, which is what lets click-to-center and the entry aim at an exact panel.

notes.label: Settle-snap inside the same glide
notes.description: Snapping redirects the target rather than the scroll. When the wheel has been quiet for 120ms and less than 60px of glide remain, the target moves once onto the nearest panel center, so the row lands on an image without a second easing curve fighting the first.

notes.label: Full-resolution offscreen buffer
notes.description: The panels render into a render target sized at device pixels, not CSS pixels; a CSS-sized target would rasterize at 1x and upscale, which reads as blur on retina once the lens resamples it.

notes.label: Aspect-driven widths
notes.description: Every panel is the same height and takes its width from the measured aspect of its texture, so nothing is cropped or stretched. Slot offsets are rebuilt as each image resolves, and the row re-centers itself until the first scroll.

notes.label: Center-out focus wave
notes.description: Panels leaving for focus are ranked by absolute distance from the focused card and grouped when those distances are within a pixel, so symmetric left and right pairs depart together. Closing reverses the ranking, so the wave returns edges-in.

entries.check: Thumbnails rise and grow into the panel row drawn through the blue-edged glass lens, the row scrolls to 03/12, a click opens the Swanhold preview, and closing returns to the carousel.

entries.name: growth-clock
entries.title: Growth Clock
entries.description: The ones digit of the wall-clock seconds, drawn as closed loops that grow, from Growth in kitasenjudesign.com/clock without its GUI. Each digit is rasterised, its outline and holes traced, and every loop resampled to a fixed node count so any digit morphs node for node into any other. Every frame splits long edges and inserts nodes at random, then relaxes them with spring, align and grid-bucketed repulsion forces plus a decaying random kick, and growth may not sink more than 3px into the glyph. When the second changes the line eases onto the next digit in 0.1s, the grown nodes are dropped, the loops flash a white fill and growth starts over. Every 10s it switches between three presets with a harder kick. Click to restart the current digit.

notes.label: Digits that morph node for node
notes.description: Every digit is traced into an outline plus up to two holes, and each loop is resampled to the same node count for all ten digits. A morph rotates the next outline to the closest match, spreads grown nodes along the chords between the original ones, then drops them once they lie on the new line, so nothing jumps.

notes.label: Growth held off the glyph
notes.description: An eroded bitmap of the digit blocks any node from moving more than 3px inside it, so the scribble piles up around the figure instead of filling it. Repulsion is bucketed on a grid the size of the repel radius, so 8000 nodes stay cheap.

notes.label: Pauses when unseen
notes.description: The loop stops offscreen and in hidden tabs and picks up at the current second. With reduced motion the plain outline of each digit swaps once a second, with no growth and no fill flash.

entries.check: The seconds digit morphs from 0 through 7 with scribbled loops growing around each glyph and resetting on the next digit.

entries.name: neon-iceberg
entries.title: Neon Iceberg
entries.description: An engraved mountain on a gridded ice block, from toolcraft.sh/demos/neon-iceberg without its control panel. One three.js mesh holds a 192 by 192 height field, four perimeter walls and four base plates, and a single vertex shader raises the peak, folds its ridges and cuts the jagged seam where rock meets ice. The fragment shader lights the rock from a low side angle and engraves it with horizontal hatching that thickens in shadow, draws a square ink grid on every wall, and prints flowing lines on the plate tops. Every two seconds the base eases apart into four plates. Drag on the iceberg to orbit it.

notes.label: One mesh, shaped on the GPU
notes.description: The geometry is a flat grid, four unit walls and four unit boxes tagged with region and slice attributes. The vertex shader turns them into the mountain, the walls up to the seam, and plates of equal thickness under the deepest recess, so every setting is a uniform and nothing is rebuilt.

notes.label: Print screens anchored to the view
notes.description: The rock hatching runs on a view-space coordinate, so strokes stay horizontal as you orbit. Each stroke is integrated over the pixel footprint, so fine lines keep their average tone instead of aliasing when small.

notes.label: Grid through the seam
notes.description: Ice that reaches up into the mountain cap is inked on the virtual cube plane along the sight ray, so grid lines continue straight through the rock and ice join.

notes.label: Orbit only on the object
notes.description: A drag starts only where the pixel under the pointer is opaque, so empty background still scrolls the page. Reduced motion holds the plates fully parted.

entries.check: The engraved iceberg block renders with the peak shading shifting, and late drags orbit the object to a tilted view.

entries.name: extrude-type
entries.title: Extrude Type
entries.description: A slab of marble with every letter cut into it. Each letter is a marble piston resting just below the surface, so at rest the text reads as an engraving. Letters near the pointer slide up out of their slots into pale towers, hold for a moment, then sink back. Three.js with a rounded-glyph instanced mesh, a per-instance height attribute, soft key lights and a warm fill, plus a 0.9px soft focus.
entries.check: Letters near the pointer rise out of the engraved text block as raised shadowed blocks and sink back as the pointer moves on.

entries.name: aura-carousel
entries.title: Aura Carousel
entries.description: Looping customer-story carousel from toolcraft.sh/demos/aura-carousel, without its control panel. The cards and their testimonials are painted once into a 2x strip texture, and one WebGL fragment shader redraws the rail from it. At each side of the viewport a stationary zone bends the cards with a stretch warp and a sideways ripple, smears them into a 20-tap spectral dispersion, adds a ragged noise-shaped aura and fades them into the page. A light band at each zone boundary flares and refracts cards as they cross it, and scroll speed adds a motion streak. Drag with the mouse, swipe a trackpad or touch, or use the arrow buttons and keys; the rail snaps to the nearest card 480ms after a wheel stops.

notes.label: The DOM rail is only the input surface
notes.description: A native horizontal scroller holds three copies of the cards for scrolling, dragging and keyboard focus. Once WebGL is ready its images and text are hidden and the shader draws everything from one wrapped scroll value, so the loop has no seam and no clone bookkeeping.

notes.label: Effects anchored to the viewport, not the cards
notes.description: Warp, dispersion, aura and edge fade are functions of screen x, so a card is clean in the middle and picks up the effect only while it passes through the outer 13% at each side.

notes.label: Painted once, sampled every frame
notes.description: Images and testimonials are drawn into two canvases at 2x and uploaded once. Frames render only while scroll or velocity changes, and the backing canvas runs at devicePixelRatio times renderScale.

notes.label: CORS images
notes.description: Card images become WebGL textures, so they must be served with CORS. If a texture cannot be built the plain DOM cards stay visible.

entries.check: Dragging moves the testimonial rail both ways and cards blur, warp and split into colour fringes as they pass the side zones.

entries.name: frosted-plate-carousel
entries.title: Frosted Plate Carousel
entries.description: A wrapping diagonal of thin image plates. Each plate is a 0.0175-thick box whose cover-fit UVs mix a sharp texture into a 64px blur across a 0.15 UV-edge smoothstep, which is the glass. X wraps on a single scroll number. Z is -X times the depth multiplier, so the row recedes on a diagonal at -PI/6. Wheel and drag shift that scroll number; hover slides the inner group; click eases rotation Y to 0, recenters X, dollies the camera from z=35 to 30, and hides the other plates. Escape or a second click reverses the same tweens. Three.js with GSAP.

notes.label: The glass is an edge mix, not transmission
notes.description: Each plate samples a sharp texture and a 64px blur through the same cover-fit UV. A 0.15 UV-edge smoothstep fades the sharp sample into the blur, and the blur's alpha is 0.75. That mix is the frost. There is no MeshPhysical glass.

notes.label: Z is slaved to X
notes.description: A single wrapped X puts every plate on a looping line. Z is -X times 1.5 times the viewport aspect on desktop, or -X times 6 on portrait, so the row recedes on a diagonal instead of orbiting a ring. Rotation Y stays at -PI/6 until a click eases it to 0.

notes.label: Click freezes the wrap
notes.description: While a plate is focused the wrap loop stops writing positions, which is what lets the GSAP tweens own X, Z, and rotation. Other plates hide by index. Escape or a second click runs the same tweens in reverse, then the wrap loop starts again.

entries.check: Plates recede on a diagonal with frosted edges, the scroll shifts the row, a click isolates one plate head-on, and the next click restores the row before it scrolls back.

entries.name: wind-drift-field
entries.title: Wind Drift Field
entries.description: Still air you stir with the pointer, running on a real fluid solver rather than a painted force field. Fourteen thousand tracers ride the velocity field and leave trails that fade back into the paper, and every trail is coloured by the speed of the air carrying it, so a slow eddy stays green and a hard sweep burns red. The air is a Stable Fluids grid and the three steps in its loop are what make it read as wind rather than as blobs. Self-advection carries the velocity field along itself, so momentum keeps travelling after your hand stops and a stroke moves downstream and stretches instead of sitting where you drew it. Pressure projection solves a Poisson equation each frame and subtracts the gradient to remove divergence, which is the step that makes air behave like air: without it velocity is created and destroyed in place, which is exactly what a stamped gust looks like, and with it the air pushed out of one place has to go somewhere, so a stroke rolls up into vortices at its ends and the flow curves around itself. Vorticity confinement puts back the small swirls the solver own interpolation smears away, and its gain is capped at half the energy viscosity removes, so a wake stays turbulent without the field ever churning forever. Nothing moves on its own: with the air at rest a tracer draws a zero-length segment and the buffer keeps fading, so the surface sits empty until it is touched, and once the kinetic energy decays the loop parks itself on a cleanly cleared buffer rather than on the residue an eight bit fade can never round away. The trail is a ping-pong pair of framebuffers, so it is never stored as history, only as what is left of the last frame. One WebGL canvas, no library and no asset required.

notes.label: Projection is what makes it air
notes.description: A gust painted straight into a velocity field has divergence: air appears in one cell and vanishes in another, which the eye reads instantly as a stamp rather than a flow. Solving each frame for the pressure whose gradient cancels that divergence, then subtracting it, forces air pushed out of one place to go somewhere. That single step is the difference between blobs and a stroke that rolls up into vortices at its ends.

notes.label: Momentum outlives the gesture
notes.description: The velocity field is advected along itself, so a stroke keeps travelling and stretching after the pointer has stopped. Nothing replays the pointer path; what you see a second later is where the air it moved has since got to.

notes.label: Turbulence cannot outrun the damping
notes.description: Vorticity confinement adds energy on purpose, to feed back the small swirls advection smears away. Left free it adds more than viscosity removes and the field churns forever, which is exactly what happened at first. The gain is capped at half the damping headroom, so coming to rest is a property of the solver rather than a lucky pair of constants.

notes.label: Colour is the air speed, not decoration
notes.description: Each segment is tinted by the speed of the flow that drew it, walked along the ramp on speed rather than speed squared so the low end is not crushed into one colour. A drifting eddy comes out green and a fast sweep saturates to red, so the palette is reading the simulation rather than sitting on top of it.

notes.label: The loop parks itself, on a clean surface
notes.description: Once the kinetic energy decays past a threshold there is nothing left to compute, so the frame callback coasts four seconds to let the trails clear and then stops. It hard-clears both buffers on the way out: an eight bit fade that mixes seven percent toward the background can never round the last level away, so parking without that clear would freeze faint residue on screen forever.

notes.label: Fixed step, by choice
notes.description: Semi-Lagrangian advection is stable at any step size, so a variable delta would not blow up, it would just make a stroke travel a different distance per frame on every machine. The solver runs on a fixed 30fps step so the flow looks the same everywhere.

entries.check: The still dark field fills with green tracer streaks that swirl into vortices behind the pointer, turning red where the sweep is fastest.

entries.name: elastic-string-field
entries.title: Elastic String Field
entries.description: A field of fat rubber ribbons that toss themselves in, shove each other apart, and settle into a packed arrangement. Each ribbon is thirty five mass points wired by two spring sets: structural springs between neighbours hold its length, and bending springs between every point and the one two along resist folding, which is what keeps it reading as a stiff band instead of a limp chain. Every point in the field also repels every other point inside the repulsion radius, walls included, so ribbons never overlap and the field distributes itself along its own cushions. A ribbon is born compressed, its points a tenth of a rest length apart along a sine wave, so the springs unpack it into a loop the moment it spawns and it arrives with a toss velocity in a random direction. New ribbons keep dropping wherever there is clearance until the field is full. Press an empty spot to add one, press a ribbon to drag it. Canvas 2D with no physics library.

notes.label: Two spring sets, not one
notes.description: Neighbour springs alone give a limp chain that collapses into a knot. The second set runs between every point and the one two along, and resisting that longer span is what stops the ribbon folding onto itself. Bend resistance is the dial between a noodle and a stiff band.

notes.label: A ribbon is tossed by its own compression
notes.description: Points spawn a tenth of a rest length apart along a sine wave, so a new ribbon is a coiled spring holding thirty five points on top of each other. The structural springs unpack it over the next few frames, which is where the flip and the loop come from. The toss velocity only decides which way it travels.

notes.label: Nothing collides, everything cushions
notes.description: There is no contact test. Points inside the repulsion radius push apart with a force that falls off linearly to zero at the edge, and the walls apply the identical cushion inward. Ribbons never overlap because they never get close enough to, and the field spaces itself without any packing pass.

notes.label: Frame-capped on purpose
notes.description: Forces are added straight to velocities in pixels per frame with no delta time anywhere, so the source's 60fps cap is part of the physics. The loop reproduces that gate rather than running free, or a 120Hz display would run the field at double speed.

entries.check: Thick coloured ribbons toss in on a blue field, push each other apart and settle into a packed arrangement.

entries.name: prism-light-instrument
entries.title: Prism Light Instrument
entries.description: A lighting rig you play with a pointer, where the light lands on a height field instead of on empty space. Typed letters, a ruled grid and a fine tooth are pressed into the surface, and every lamp rakes across that relief at a shallow angle, because grazing light is what makes an emboss read. The beam is measured rather than painted: three angular gaussians per lamp, one per wavelength, offset by a fixed chromatic amount around an achromatic core, multiplied by a two-term radial throw and gelled from tungsten through neutral to daylight. Standing on the surface is a real triangle of glass. Rays are traced through it in the vertex shader with a wavelength-dependent index, refracting in one face and out another, following the bounce when a ray hits the far wall too steeply to leave, so the spectrum is the actual dispersion of that geometry and not a gradient laid over it. Each pair of adjacent rays spans a quad rather than drawing a line, so the fan is watertight in a single frame instead of filling in over time, and a flat-topped profile across each slice sums to one however wide it spreads, which is what keeps a widening fan from banding at every seam. The glass casts a soft shadow because the lamp is a disc rather than a point: the penumbra falls out of the silhouette geometry, so it carries no temporal noise at all. Both the direct beams and the refracted spectrum answer to the same baked normal and openness map, so the colour carves the letters and finds the ruling rather than sitting on top of the picture. Letters slide to re-centre and sink to depth on their own clocks, a running average converges the image over twenty-six samples, and an ordered dither keeps the long dark falloff from banding into eight bits. One WebGL2 canvas, no library and no asset required.

notes.label: The light lands on relief, not on a backdrop
notes.description: Type, a ruled grid, a slow swell and a fine tooth are pressed into a height field, and its normals plus an openness term are baked to a texture whenever the surface changes. Both the lamps and the refracted spectrum read that same map, so the colour carves the letters instead of sitting on top of them, and the foot of a letter goes dark because its own walls are in the way rather than because it was shaded darker.

notes.label: The spectrum is traced, not painted
notes.description: A triangle of glass stands on the surface and rays are refracted through it in the vertex shader with a wavelength-dependent index, following total internal reflection when a ray cannot leave through the far wall. Adjacent rays span a quad rather than a line, so the fan is complete in one frame, and two edge rays are only allowed to bound a slice when they took the same path through the glass.

notes.label: A finite source, so the shadow has a real penumbra
notes.description: The lamp is a disc rather than a point, and the softness is solved from the silhouette geometry instead of sampled over time. The blur is identical every frame, converged or not, so dragging the glass never shows the noise a stochastic soft shadow would.

notes.label: Converged over time, but never stalled
notes.description: A running average accumulates twenty-six jittered samples and restarts on any input. While letters are still sinking the wavelength count drops to eight, since every band is full-screen overdraw, and the caustic renders at half resolution because a blurred spectrum survives it perfectly well.

notes.label: Scoped to its own box
notes.description: The original was a whole-page instrument bound to window. This version sizes from a ResizeObserver on its own root and takes keyboard only while focused, so it fills a bounded demo stage or the full screen with no branch between the two.

entries.check: Typed letters spell LIGHT blank into the embossed surface under raking coloured beams, and the last drag throws a new spectrum fan across the letters.

entries.name: monogram-morph-page
entries.title: Monogram Morph Page
entries.description: A single-viewport portfolio home where the wordmark is liquid. The mark is HTML text run through a goo filter, a gaussian blur followed by a steep alpha threshold, so crowding the letters fuses them into one blob and spreading them tears that blob into droplets which snap back into glyphs. One effect carries the whole site: on load a monogram melts and spreads into the full wordmark, and on every route change the current word melts and resolves into the next one, the swap hidden inside the mass while it is fully liquid. The mark is built as two passes of the same word through two goo filters: behind, a fat same-colour stroke that becomes the bright smear; in front, the letterforms themselves, solid and set light, sitting inside it. Each filter repaints its thresholded silhouette with a flat flood, because a gaussian blur works on premultiplied alpha and boosting alpha alone leaves the colour channels part-way to transparent. Around it, all running text is pre-split to characters and faded on a baked GSAP CustomBounce curve with a randomised stagger, so text does not fade, it flickers out and stutters back in. The bottom bar blends in exclusion and inverts, staying legible as the yellow mark passes beneath it, its active pill fills on a 1.2 second ease while its own letters flicker, and the landing route scatters draggable tags along the edges of the mark with collision rejection. Set in PangeaAfrikan where licensed, falling back to Hanken Grotesk, the one free grotesque sharing its binocular double-storey g. Live clock, container-query layout, GSAP only.

notes.label: One liquid mark does the loading and the routing
notes.description: The wordmark is HTML text pushed through a goo filter: a gaussian blur, then an alpha matrix steep enough to snap the soft edges back to a hard silhouette. Crowd the letters and they fuse into one blob; spread them and the blob tears into droplets that resolve into glyphs. The loader is that effect run from a monogram to the full wordmark, and a route change is the same effect run from one word to the next. There is no second transition vocabulary anywhere on the page.

notes.label: Two passes, two filters, and a flat flood
notes.description: Behind sits a fat same-colour stroke that the goo turns into the bright smear; in front sit the letterforms themselves, solid and set light, not an outline. They need separate filters because one blur radius wide enough to fuse the smear would dissolve the letters inside it, so the ink runs at roughly a third of the halo's blur. Each filter then repaints its thresholded silhouette with a flat flood: a gaussian blur operates on premultiplied alpha, so boosting alpha alone leaves the colour channels part-way to transparent and the mark composites washed out.

notes.label: The swap hides inside the melt
notes.description: Outgoing and incoming words cross over between 44 and 56 percent of the morph, which sits inside the plateau where blur is at maximum. Their alphas composite above the filter's threshold across the overlap, so the mass never thins at the handover: it reads as one body reshaping rather than as two words dissolving through each other.

notes.label: Text flickers rather than fades
notes.description: Every character fade eases on GSAP's CustomBounce at strength 0.8, applied to opacity rather than to position, so a character overshoots to solid, drops back to 36 percent, and stutters to rest. CustomBounce is a paid Club plugin but only a generator, so its output path is baked into bounce-ease.ts and evaluated directly. Same curve, nothing to register.

notes.label: The bar reads over anything beneath it
notes.description: The bottom nav blends in exclusion and inverts, so it stays legible whether the yellow mark, the white ground, or a droplet mid-flight is passing under it. The active pill fills over 1.2 seconds while its own letters flicker in on a tighter per-character stagger, and the inactive pills roll a fill up from below that flattens its corners on the way in.

notes.label: Sized to its container, not to the viewport
notes.description: The root declares container-type: inline-size and every length is in cqw, so the same component fills a bounded demo card and a full screen with no branch between them. That containment also makes the root the containing block for its own chrome, so the nav and the mark stay inside the component instead of escaping to the document.

entries.check: The B monogram melts into the Blank wordmark, then each nav click liquefies it into Projects and then Archive while the lists flicker in.

entries.name: colourist-reel-page
entries.title: Colourist Reel Page
entries.description: A one-screen portfolio for a film colourist, ported from the compiled source of a working colourist's site. Home is a single sentence whose role word takes its hue from the cursor's position across the page, while the reel waits as a 64px peek at the bottom edge with its own frames drawn at an eighth of their size into a canvas blurred by 100px, so the footage's colour spills up as a glow. Scroll, click or press an arrow key and the reel lifts to full bleed. Projects open as a vertical looping embla list driven by wheel gestures, where each row's opacity falls off by its distance from centre and the centred row grows a colour swatch, or as a 3-column grid whose cards swap their still for the clip on hover. Any project plays edge to edge with a seek bar, mute and timecode that fade after two idle seconds, plus a gallery and a credits view. P, I and Escape move between screens. Ships with BLANK footage on Blob and the source's Booton Medium face.

notes.label: Loop-aware row falloff
notes.description: Each list row's opacity comes from its distance to centre in slide units, read from embla's scroll progress and loop points, then eased through 1, 0.6, 0.35, 0.2, 0.12 and 0.06 to zero at six rows.

notes.label: Ambient glow from the clip
notes.description: The playing frame is drawn at an eighth of its size into a canvas that CSS blurs by 100px and saturates by 1.5, so the peeking reel lights the white page with its own colour.

notes.label: Fits its box
notes.description: Viewport units from the source are container units on the root and fixed layers are contained by a transform, so the page runs the same in a studio frame as full screen.

entries.check: The role word changes colour as the pointer crosses the page above a glowing reel peek, and a click lifts the reel into a full dark player.

entries.name: iris-outro-footer
entries.title: Iris Outro Footer
entries.description: A closing-title iris scrubbed by scroll. Five concentric discs sit locked to the centre of a sticky, clipped stage, each starting part-grown at a staggered scale and reaching full size together, so the gap between neighbours widens as the footer arrives and the target blooms outward from the middle. Ring opacity rides the same progress, the stage fades up over the last 70 percent of the range, and the sign-off unblurs into the dark centre at the end. No animation library: progress is one scroll-derived custom property and the discs interpolate their own scale in CSS.

notes.label: The stagger is the whole effect
notes.description: All five discs finish at scale 1 together but start at 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2 and 0. Because the outer disc has the least distance to travel and the innermost has the most, the bands spread apart as progress runs and the target reads as blooming outward. Give every disc the same start and it collapses into one flat zoom.

notes.label: Discs are sized against width, then clipped
notes.description: Each disc is a percentage of the stage width with a 1:1 aspect ratio, so on any landscape viewport the outer ones are taller than the stage and get cut off by its clip. That overflow is intentional: it is what makes the outer band read as a field rather than a circle sitting in the middle of the screen.

notes.label: Three separate opacity ramps
notes.description: Ring opacity is base times progress, the stage fades up only over the last 70 percent, and the sign-off resolves over the last 45 percent with its blur. They are deliberately out of phase, so the iris is already moving before it is visible and the line lands after the motion settles.

notes.label: No animation library
notes.description: Scroll writes one custom property and CSS interpolates each disc from its own start scale. The scroll listener is passive and rAF-coalesced, and reduced-motion pins progress at 1 so the closing frame is composed rather than animated.

entries.check: Concentric red rings bloom outward as the footer arrives, the That's all Folks sign-off unblurs in the centre, and scrolling back fades the iris away.

entries.name: video-summagator
entries.title: Video Summagator
entries.description: A clip turned into a solid you can orbit. The video is sampled into 96, 160 or 240 evenly spaced frames and stacked along Z as one Data3DTexture, so width and height stay the picture while depth becomes running time. A GLSL3 ray-marcher reads that cube under an orthographic camera: parallel rays, so the origin is projected back onto the camera plane rather than taken from the camera position. The selected frame splits the volume in two, everything after it opaque and everything before it accumulating over 160 steps, which is why scrubbing slides a solid surface through a smear instead of dissolving it. That surface gets a 1px outline measured in CSS pixels from four projected corners, so it holds its weight at any zoom. Viewers can drop in their own mp4 and it never leaves the browser: frames are seeked, drawn to a canvas and read back on-device. It ships no control panel of its own: every live value is a prop and every one-shot action is a method on the ref, so the controls live wherever the host puts them.

notes.label: Depth is time, so the cube is the clip
notes.description: The frames are not planes drawn one behind another. They are one Data3DTexture of w x h x frames, which lets the shader read any (x, y, time) with a single texture fetch. Everything else follows from that: the smear you see through the front face is real integration along the view ray, not a stack of alpha-blended quads.

notes.label: The selected frame is a boundary, not a sprite
notes.description: Everything from the playhead onward is treated as opaque and its boundary plane is intersected analytically, so the march ends exactly on it rather than stepping past it. That is why the surface stays crisp at any density and why scrubbing slides a solid through the haze instead of fading one image into another.

notes.label: The rays are parallel, so the origin is recomputed
notes.description: Under an orthographic camera every ray shares a direction, taken from the view matrix's third column. Starting each ray at cameraPosition, as a perspective setup would, fans them out and skews the volume. Each fragment is projected back onto the camera plane first.

notes.label: Sampling is 240 serial seeks, so the volume grows while you wait
notes.description: No browser API hands you every frame, so each sample is a seek, a drawImage and a getImageData. The texture is uploaded before the loop and re-uploaded as frames land, which is why the cube extrudes along Z during import rather than appearing at the end.

notes.label: The outline is measured in CSS pixels
notes.description: The frame's four corners are projected to screen space each draw and handed to the shader, which strokes 1 CSS px inside the edge. Doing it in world space would make the line thicken as you zoom in and vanish as you zoom out.

notes.label: The 3D texture is sRGB but declared NoColorSpace
notes.description: No sRGB internal format for 3D textures is safe across drivers, so the bytes go up raw and linearRGB decodes them in the shader. Letting three.js tag the texture sRGB double-decodes and washes the volume out.

entries.check: The clip extrudes into a 3D volume inside the wireframe cube and turns in two directions under the drags, showing the smeared time depth.
